title: Balak: only the word I'm given (Numbers 22:38)
hookLine: Balaam can speak only the word God puts in his mouth
tomorrow: Balak: how goodly are thy tents

lines: A TOAST, A REFERENCE, A FEW WORDS.
BALAK MEETS HIM AT THE BORDER.
cards: You've been asked to give a toast, or write a reference, or say a few words at a meeting, and the person asking has made it very clear what they'd like you to say. Maybe they've even done you a favor.
And what they want said isn't quite true. Balaam arrives in Moab in exactly that spot. King Balak meets him at the border, a little annoyed that he took so long, and promises him honor and reward.
Everyone knows what the king is paying for. And Balaam's first words set the terms.

teach.h: ONLY THE WORD GOD PUTS IN MY MOUTH.
teach.b: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, Balaam says: "the word that God putteth in my mouth, that shall I speak."
He'd already told Balak's messengers something like it: even if the king gave me his house full of silver and gold, I couldn't go beyond the word of God. Then comes something close to comedy.
Balak takes him up to a high place, builds seven altars, offers sacrifices, and waits for a curse.
Balaam opens his mouth, and out comes this: "How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?" Balak is beside himself: I brought you here to curse my enemies, and you've blessed them.
So he tries another hilltop, the top of Pisgah. Seven more altars. Maybe from a new angle, the curse will come.
It doesn't. Balaam says, in paraphrase, God has blessed, and I cannot turn it back. Then a third place, Peor.
Three hilltops, twenty-one altars, and not one curse.

teach.h: A NEW VIEW DOESN'T CHANGE THE TRUTH.
teach.b: A new view doesn't change what's true. The rabbis didn't treat Balaam as a hero for this.
Rashi notices that, of all things, he brings up silver and gold, and reads it as a man who wanted the money and simply couldn't get around the word. That's what makes the scene interesting.
In the story, whatever was in his heart, his mouth was held to what God gave him, and the curse that was bought and paid for turned into a blessing.

how: Balaam's oracles are read in the portion of Balak each summer, and Jewish commentators, starting with Rashi, read his words alongside the question of what was really in his heart.

games.q: you're Balaam. Balak has brought you to a new hilltop, built seven altars, and is waiting for his curse. what comes out?
o: a blessing: how shall I curse whom God hath not cursed?
games.why: a blessing, three times over. a new view didn't change what was true.

practice: Run through the conversations ahead of you today and find one where you might say what someone wants to hear instead of what's so: a compliment you don't mean, a promise you can't keep, a yes that's really a no.
Find the true sentence you could say instead, kind and plain, and hold it; you don't need to be harsh, only true.

wordCard.voice: Balak. The king who moved his hired seer from hilltop to hilltop, hoping for a curse, and got only the word God gave.
